paragraphs: “Gentlemen of the jury, the pile of facts is not the only thing that threatens my client with ruin,” he began. “What truly condemns him is a single fact: the dead body of his father. Suppose this were an ordinary murder. You would throw out the charge, because the evidence is trivial, incomplete and fantastic once you examine each piece on its own. Or at least you would hesitate before destroying a man’s life only on account of the prejudice against him, which he has, sadly, earned only too well. But this is no ordinary murder. It is parricide. That grips men’s minds so hard that the evidence, trivial and incomplete as it is, begins to look less trivial and less incomplete, even to a mind free of prejudice. How can such a prisoner be acquitted? What if he did commit the murder and walks away unpunished? That is the thought every person in this room feels in his heart, almost without willing it, by sheer instinct.

“Yes, it is a fearful thing to shed a father’s blood. He is the father who gave me life and loved me, who held nothing back for my sake, who grieved over my illnesses from my earliest years, who spent his whole life worrying about my happiness and who lived in my joys and my successes. To murder such a father is unthinkable. Gentlemen of the jury, what is a father—a true father? What does that great word mean? What great idea lies in that name? We have already said in part what a true father is and what he ought to be. In the case that so occupies us, and over which our hearts ache, the father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, did not fit the idea of a father that we have just described. That is the misfortune. And some fathers truly are a misfortune. Let us look at this misfortune a little more closely. Given the weight of the decision before you, we must shrink from nothing. It is our special duty not to shrink from any idea, like children or frightened women, as the talented prosecutor happily phrased it.

“But in his heated speech my esteemed opponent (and he was my opponent before I had said a word) cried out several times, ‘Oh, I will not give up the defense of the prisoner to the lawyer who has come down from Petersburg. I accuse, but I defend also!’ He cried that out several times, yet he forgot something. This terrible prisoner was grateful for twenty-three years for a mere pound of nuts, given to him by the only person who had been kind to him as a child in his father’s house. Might not such a man well have remembered for those twenty-three years how he ran around his father’s backyard ‘without boots on his feet and with his little trousers hanging by one button’—the words of the kind-hearted Doctor Herzenstube?

“Oh, gentlemen of the jury, why must we look at this misfortune any closer? Why repeat what we all know? What did my client find when he came here, to his father’s house? And why portray him as a heartless egoist and a monster? He is uncontrolled, wild and unruly. That is what we are trying him for. But who is to blame for the life he has led? Who is to blame that his upbringing was so improper, despite his excellent nature and his grateful, sensitive heart? Did anyone teach him to be reasonable? Did study ever enlighten him? Did anyone, even in his childhood, love him the least bit? My client was left to Providence like a beast of the field. Perhaps, after long years of separation, he longed to see his father. A thousand times, perhaps, as he thought back on his childhood, he drove off the loathsome phantoms that haunted his childish dreams, and with all his heart he longed to embrace his father and forgive him! And what met him? Cynical jeers, suspicions, and squabbling over money. Day after day over the brandy he heard nothing but revolting talk and vicious maxims. In the end he watched his father lure his mistress away from him, and with his own money too. Oh, gentlemen of the jury, how cruel and revolting that was! And all the while that old man complained about his son’s disrespect and cruelty. He slandered him in society, harmed him, blackened his name, and bought up his unpaid debts in order to get him thrown into prison.

“Gentlemen of the jury, men like my client look fierce, unruly and uncontrolled on the surface, yet they are often—indeed most often—exceedingly tender-hearted. They simply do not show it. Do not laugh, do not laugh at my idea! The talented prosecutor mocked my client without mercy just now for loving Schiller, for loving the sublime and the beautiful! In his place I would not have laughed at that. Yes, such natures—oh, let me speak in their defense, they are so often and so cruelly misunderstood—such natures often hunger for tenderness, goodness and justice, as a contrast to their own unruliness and ferocity, and they hunger for it without realizing. On the surface they are passionate and fierce, but they are painfully capable of loving a woman, for instance, with a spiritual and exalted love. Again I say, do not laugh at me. This is very often so with such natures. But they cannot hide their passions, some of them very coarse, and those show and are noticed, while the man within stays unseen. Their passions burn out fast. Yet beside a noble and lofty person, this seemingly coarse and rough man looks for a new life. He tries to mend himself, to be better, to become noble and honorable, ‘sublime and beautiful,’ however much people have ridiculed the phrase.

“I said a moment ago that I would not dare to touch on my client’s engagement. But I may say half a word. What we heard just now was not evidence. It was the scream of a frenzied woman bent on revenge. And it was not for her—oh, not for her!—to accuse him of treachery, because she is the one who betrayed him! Had she had a little time to think, she would never have given such testimony. Oh, do not believe her! No, my client is not the monster she called him!

“On the eve of His Crucifixion the Lover of Mankind said: ‘I am the Good Shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep, so that not one of them might be lost.’ Let no man’s soul be lost through us!

“A moment ago I asked what the word ‘father’ means, and I cried out that it is a great word and a precious name. But we must use words honestly, gentlemen, and I will dare to call things by their right names. A father like old Karamazov cannot be called a father, and he does not deserve the name. Filial love for an unworthy father is an absurdity, an impossibility. Love cannot be made from nothing. Only God can make something from nothing.

“‘Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath,’ the apostle writes, out of a heart glowing with love. I do not quote these sacred words for my client’s sake. I mention them for the sake of all fathers. Who has given me authority to preach to fathers? No one. But as a man and a citizen I make my appeal—_vivos voco!_ We are not long on this earth. We do many evil deeds and speak many evil words. So let us all take hold of a good moment, while we are together, to say a kind word to one another. That is what I am doing. Since I am standing here, I am using my chance. It is not for nothing that the highest authority has given us this tribune—all Russia hears us! I am not speaking only to the fathers who are present. I cry out to all fathers: ‘Fathers, provoke not your children to wrath.’ Yes, let us first carry out Christ’s command ourselves, and only then dare to expect it from our children. Otherwise we are not fathers but enemies to our children, and they are not our children but our enemies, and we ourselves have made them so. ‘What measure ye mete it shall be measured unto you again’—I am not the one saying this; it is the precept of the Gospel: measure out to others what they measure out to you. How can we blame children if they measure us by our own measure?

“Not long ago, in Finland, a servant girl was suspected of having secretly given birth to a child. She was kept under watch, and in the corner of the loft, behind some bricks, they found a box that nobody had known about. They opened it, and inside lay the body of a newborn baby, which she had killed. In the same box were the skeletons of two more babies. By her own confession she had killed them as soon as they were born.

“Gentlemen of the jury, was she a mother to her children? She bore them, true. But was she a mother to them? Would anyone dare to give her the sacred name of mother? Let us be bold, gentlemen. Let us even be audacious. At this moment it is our duty, and we must not be afraid of certain words and ideas, as the Moscow women in Ostrovsky’s play are, who take fright at the sound of certain words. No, let us show that the progress of recent years has reached even us, and let us say it plainly: a father is not merely the man who begets the child, but the man who begets it and does his duty by it.

“Oh, of course, there is another meaning, another reading of the word ‘father,’ which insists that any father, even a monster, even an enemy of his children, remains my father simply because he begot me. But this is, so to say, the mystical meaning. My intellect cannot grasp it. I can only accept it by faith, or better, _on faith_, as I accept many other things that I do not understand but which religion tells me to believe. In that case, let it stay outside the sphere of actual life. That sphere has its own rights, but it also lays great duties and obligations on us. In that sphere, if we want to be humane—Christian, in fact—we must, or ought to, act only on convictions that reason and experience can justify, convictions that have been through the crucible of analysis. In a word, we must act rationally, not as if in a dream or a delirium, so that we do no harm and do not mistreat and ruin a man. Then it will be real Christian work, not only mystical but rational and philanthropic....”
